By the end you can draw a separate diagram for each collision, carry each signed velocity into the next collision and decide whether the particles will collide again.

scenes.text: A multiple -collision question follows what happens after the first impact. A particle might then hit a wall, or a third particle. Deal with each collision separately, because each changes the velocities. Draw a fresh, clearly labelled diagram. Give each new unknown a different name, so you carry the right velocity forward. For a wall, use the rebound information given. The particle's momentum alone is not conserved.

scenes.text: Consider three spheres moving right along a smooth track. A is behind B, and C is further ahead. A catches B. After that impact, A moves more slowly, while B goes ahead and catches C. C moves off and B slows down. A is still behind B. Our question is whether A will catch B again. First picture those two impacts, then we'll calculate what changes.

C moves off and B slows down. A is still behind B. Our question is whether A will catch B again. First picture those two impacts; then we'll calculate what changes.

scenes.text: Now collision one. Find B's velocity after A hits it. Right is positive. Let's get drawing. A, one kilogram, four metres per second. B, two kilograms, three metres per second. Afterwards A moves at two metres per second. Call B's new velocity v B. The pair's momentum is conserved because no external force changes its total. Before equals after. One times four, plus two times three, equals one times two, plus two v B. Ten equals two plus two v B. Subtract two and divide by two. v B is four metres per second. Positive means right. Carry that four forward, not the original three.

scenes.text: Same direction. The one behind must be faster than the one in front. What if both move left? Can they collide? Yes. B is behind. Faster left means more negative, because right is positive. With A left of B, A's signed velocity must be greater for the gap to close. You can draw a separate diagram for each collision, carry each signed velocity into the next collision, and decide whether the particles will collide again.

scenes.text: Now, collision two. B hits C. Find B's new velocity. Use the result just found. Let's get drawing. Two kilograms, now four metres per second. C. Three kilograms, one metre per second. Afterwards C moves at three metres per second. Call B's new velocity. W B. V B belonged to the first collision. Conserve this pair's momentum. Two times four, plus three times one, equals two w B, plus three times three. Eleven equals two w B plus nine. Subtract nine and divide by two. W B is one metre per second. Now, will they collide again? A is behind B. A moves right at two metres per second. B at one. Two is greater than one. The one behind is faster, so the gap closes. Yes, A catches B again.
